etymology_text: From Old English catt (“male cat”), catte (“female cat”), this is in turn from Proto-Germanic *kattuz.

examples.text: Thow we hadde ykuld þe Cat / ȝut shulde ther come another / To crache vs and alle oure kynde / thogh we crope vnder benches
examples.ref: c. 1390, [William Langland], “[Prologue]”, in Peres plouhman (X, C-text), southwest Worcestershire, published c. 1395, folio 3, verso; republished as MS. HM 143, San Marino, CA: Huntingdon Digital Library, p. 2011:
examples.english: "If we'd killed the cat, there should nevertheless be another [one] / to snatch us and all of our kind / even if we crept underneath [the] benches."
examples.translation: "If we'd killed the cat, there should nevertheless be another [one] / to snatch us and all of our kind / even if we crept underneath [the] benches."

etymology_text: From Old English word, from Proto-West Germanic *word, from Proto-Germanic *wurdą, from Proto-Indo-European *werdʰom. Doublet of verbe.

examples.text: Ȝe knowe ek that in fourme of ſpeche is chaunge / With-inne a thousand ȝeer, and wordes tho / That hadden pris now wonder nyce and ſtraunge / Us thenketh hem, and ȝet thei ſpake hem so / And ſpedde as wel in loue as men now do
examples.ref: a. 1400, Geoffrey Chaucer, “Book II”, in Troilus and Criseyde, lines 22–28:
examples.english: You also know that the form of language is in flux; / within a thousand years, words / that had currency; really weird and bizarre / they seem to us now, but they still spoke them / and accomplished as much in love as men do now.
examples.translation: You also know that the form of language is in flux; / within a thousand years, words / that had currency; really weird and bizarre / they seem to us now, but they still spoke them / and accomplished as much in love as men do now.
